attributes: The crab plans a series of tricks to acquire food: it has a taste for oysters, but the oyster's flesh is walled in two very strong shells, and the crab lacks the strength to open them — and risks a claw if the shell shuts on it. So the crab resorts to strategy: it watches for the moment the oyster, safe out of the wind in the sun's rays, opens its shell to take the air; then, stealthily inserting a pebble, it stops the oyster from closing, inserts its claws in safety, and feeds on the flesh inside. There are two kinds of crab, river and sea. Ten crabs bound with a handful of basil will gather all the scorpions of the neighbourhood (the charm, stated twice). The account's moral: evil men do likewise, feasting on others' troubles by stealth.

attributes: The maritime urchin is small, worthless and contemptible to look at, yet seafarers take it as a sign of storm or calm. When it senses a stormy blast coming, it seizes a good-sized pebble and carries it as ballast, dragging it like an anchor lest the swell throw it up; thus it saves itself not by its own strength but by borrowed weight. Sailors, seeing this, take precautions. Men with all their astronomy are often deceived by the sky; the urchin is not mistaken — the significance of the signs it sees does not escape it. The account concludes this foresight is a gift of the Lord, who has left no creature without knowledge.

attributes: The tortoise, testudo, is named because it is covered by the vault of its shell, in the manner of an arched roof. There are four species: land, sea, mud — that is, living in swamps or marshland — and a fourth belonging to rivers, in fresh water. Some relate the incredible fact that ships sail more slowly when they carry the right foot of a tortoise. (The account itself labels that last claim incredible.)

attributes: Frogs, rane, get their name from their constant chatter (garrulitas), croaking all around the marshes where they breed, 'calling out in an uncouth manner with their peculiar sound'. Of their kinds: some are water frogs, others marsh frogs; some are called toads, rubete, because they live in brambles (rubus) — they are larger than the others; others are calamites, living among reeds (calamus) and bushes, the smallest of all, and green.
